title: Ovid Well Depth and Drilling Cost Guide
meta_description: Ovid wells have a 64 ft median depth, 20 ft median water level, and typical finished costs of $8,200-$15,500.
h1: What Ovid, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Ovid means checking more than whether a well is already drilled. Permit records show a mostly shallow plains well area, with a median reported depth of 64 feet and a median static water level of 20 feet. Reported yields are generally strong, but the records are uneven: 553 wells are listed, while 45 report a pump yield and 21 report a static water level.

This page covers wells within 5 miles of Ovid in Sedgwick County, including nearby rural areas toward Julesburg and Sedgwick. Use the local numbers to screen a property, then verify the specific permit, well construction, pump, water quality, and legal use before closing.

sections.heading: Ovid well depths stay shallow, but not every lot is the same
sections.html:
Ovid’s reported well depth has a median of 64 feet, with the middle half between 49 and 90 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate: many bids should be based on a relatively shallow hole, not an assumed deep Front Range well. Still, the spread matters. The 90th-percentile depth is 149 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 502 feet.

Depth records show 77% of wells under 100 feet, 21% between 100 and 300 feet, and 2% between 300 and 600 feet. Local ground is described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. A driller will still need to account for the exact lot, nearby logs, casing and grout requirements, and the possibility that the first water-bearing zone is not adequate.

sections.heading: What Ovid wells produce for homes and livestock
sections.html:
Among the 45 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 50.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 14.0 to 800.0 gallons per minute, which is a very wide range. Most reported wells are productive: 73% show yields of 15 gallons per minute or more, 24% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 2% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

That does not guarantee a particular parcel. Yield figures may represent different testing methods and uses, and only a portion of the constructed wells reports a yield. Ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage capacity, and actual recovery behavior. A household may need less than a stock or irrigation well, but a strong reported area average is not a substitute for testing the well you will own.

sections.heading: Ovid water levels are shallow, but the trend is not proven
sections.html:
The 21 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 20 feet, with the middle half from 10 to 27 feet. For excavation and well planning, that suggests water may be encountered relatively close to the surface in many parts of the Ovid area. It also means a contractor should consider shallow groundwater when planning trenching, drainage, and equipment access.

The permit history does not establish a falling water table. The available static-water sample is small, and the records provided do not give a water-level series by decade. Do not treat the 20-foot median as a guaranteed pumping level. A current measurement, neighboring well logs, seasonal conditions, and a pump test are more useful for judging the individual property.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Ovid and when permits were issued
sections.html:
The permit record goes back to the 1950s and includes a newest permit year of 2024. Permit counts were 73 in the 1950s, 44 in the 1960s, 35 in the 1970s, 47 in the 1980s, 45 in the 1990s, 98 in the 2000s, 15 in the 2010s, and 18 in the 2020s. That history shows long-standing well use around Ovid, with many older wells mixed with newer construction.

The most active drillers in these records are Jim Feighny & Sons, listed as Feighny, Jim, with 77 wells; Haggard Drilling Inc., listed as Haggard, Kenneth W, with 35; and Stewart Drilling Co., listed as Stewart, Dennis W., with 31. Treat those names as permit-history context, not a guarantee of present availability or workmanship.

sections.heading: What a new Ovid well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
For Ovid’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35-$55 per foot. At the local median depth of 64 feet, the drilled hole itself is modeled at about $2,200-$3,500. That is not the complete project price. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at approximately $8,200-$15,500.

Use the depth range when comparing bids. A property that needs 149 feet or more can cost more than the median-depth example, and an unusual 502-foot well shows that deeper outcomes are possible. Get a written scope identifying casing, grout, development, pump size, tank, electrical work, trenching, water testing, and permit-related work. Confirm what happens if the first hole has inadequate yield or requires additional depth.

sections.heading: Ovid property risks: water quality, septic, and building plans
sections.html:
Four mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites are located within about 10 miles of Ovid. The records show no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that area. Those facts do not certify a private well as safe. Test the water after a purchase and after any change in land use, with testing selected for the site and the intended household use.

Low yield is not the only concern. Review the well’s construction, pump, storage, static level, and maintenance history. Before building, confirm the separation and layout requirements for the well, septic system, replacement area, drive, and house. Domestic and household wells make up 34% of the records, stock wells 22%, irrigation wells 29%, and monitoring wells 6%, so the nearby well’s permitted use may not match your plans. Check DWR records and current county requirements before relying on an old permit.

sections.heading: A practical Ovid checklist before you buy or build
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the area median. Pull the Colorado DWR permit and completion records, confirm the permitted use, compare nearby logs in Ovid and toward Julesburg or Sedgwick, and ask for recent water-quality and pump information. If the property has no well, have a local driller review neighboring depths before setting a budget. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable, even though this area is described mainly as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock.

For a new build, price the complete water system rather than drilling alone. Include the pump, tank, electrical service, trenching, septic work, access, and testing. If the intended use involves irrigation or other demands beyond the permit, confirm the legal water supply first. Colorado DWR rules, exempt household-use limits, and basin requirements can affect what you may legally pump. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ovid, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Ovid is 64 feet, and the middle half runs from 49 to 90 feet. About 77% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depths vary, however: the 90th percentile is 149 feet and the deepest recorded well is 502 feet. Neighboring completion reports are useful, but they do not guarantee the depth on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ovid?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 64-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,200-$3,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,200-$15,500. Ask bidders what is included and how they handle extra depth, poor yield, casing, grout, testing, and site access.

faq.q: How much water do Ovid wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 45 Ovid-area wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 50.0 gallons per minute, with a middle range of 14.0 to 800.0 gallons per minute. Reported results show 73% at 15 gallons per minute or more. The sample is limited, so verify the specific well’s test, recovery, pump, tank, and permitted use before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ovid, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit map shows 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, but that does not determine the quality of an individual well. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, especially before drinking it. Review the well construction and location relative to septic and other potential sources. A permit record alone is not a drinking-water certification.

faq.q: What is the water level in an Ovid well?
faq.a: The median reported static water level near Ovid is 20 feet below ground, with the middle half between 10 and 27 feet. Only 21 wells report a static water level, and the available facts do not establish a decline by decade. Use a current measurement and a pump test for the property rather than assuming every well will have water at the median depth.
